name: Sustainable Crop and Horticultural Production
objectives: On one of your own plots, check the soil's health in the field and describe how to take a good sample for a soil test, naming at least three signs of healthy or poor soil

For one field crop and one vegetable, choose certified seed or clean planting material, the spacing and the planting or transplanting date, with each choice taken from a dealer, extension or the seed packet
For your main field crop, write a feeding plan that combines organic matter, legumes and well-placed fertilizer, with rates marked as coming from a soil test or extension

Given a crop with pests or disease, scout it on a weekly routine, choose IPM actions and use a registered pesticide only by its label when justified, starting with prevention and non-chemical controls
For a small vegetable plot, plan efficient watering with drip or cans, mulch and the right time of day, checking soil moisture before each watering
At harvest, plan how to harvest, sort, dry and store produce to cut losses, with the right maturity, gentle handling and safe storage for each crop

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Know your soil
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Check your soil's health in the field and know when and how to get a soil test.
This lesson builds toward: On one of your own plots, you will check the soil's health in the field and describe how to take a good sample for a soil test, naming at least three signs of healthy or poor soil.
Healthy soil is dark, crumbly, smells earthy, has earthworms and roots that go deep, and soaks up rain instead of letting it run off. Poor soil is hard, pale, crusts after rain, or stays waterlogged. Do a simple field check: dig a hole a spade deep, look at the colour and layers, squeeze a handful, count worms, and watch where water runs or stands after rain.
A soil test tells you what your eyes cannot: acidity (pH) and the main nutrients. Many soils in high-rainfall parts of Kenya and Nigeria are acidic, which locks up nutrients; liming may be advised. Ask your extension officer, research institute or agrovet where to get a soil test and how to take a good sample: many small samples from across the plot, mixed together, not from manure heaps or burned spots.
Build soil health every season: add organic matter (manure, compost, crop residues), keep the soil covered, rotate crops, and avoid burning and needless ploughing.
Step by step:
- Dig a spade-deep hole and look at colour, layers and roots.
- Squeeze a handful; count earthworms.
- Watch where water runs off or stands.
- Ask extension or an agrovet where to get a soil test.
- Take many small samples across the plot and mix them.
Words to know:
- Soil health: the ability of soil to grow strong plants, hold water and support life.
- pH: a measure of how acidic or alkaline the soil is; many crops prefer slightly acidic to neutral soil.
- Organic matter: decayed plant and animal material in soil, such as manure and compost.
- Liming: adding lime to reduce soil acidity.
Official sources:
- Kenya Agricultural and Livestock Research Organization (KALRO)
- FAO: Climate-Smart Agriculture Sourcebook (soil and water management)
Try it now: Do the field check on one plot: dig, look, squeeze, count worms, and write what you found. Then find out where you can get a soil test near you and what it costs.
You can now check your soil's health in the field and know how to take a sample for a soil test.

check.q: After rain, water stands on your plot for days and the soil is pale and hard. What does this show?
options: Very healthy soil
Soil that needs care, such as more organic matter
Soil that needs no change
Soil with too many earthworms
check.why: Healthy soil is dark and crumbly and soaks up rain; standing water and hard, pale soil are signs of poor soil.

check.q: You are taking a soil sample. Where do you dig?
options: Only next to the manure heap
Only where you burned residues
One spot in the middle of the plot
Many small spots across the plot, mixed together
check.why: Many small samples mixed together show the whole plot; manure heaps and burned spots give wrong results.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Planting right: seed, spacing and timing
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Plant a field crop and raise vegetable seedlings with good seed, spacing and timing.
This lesson builds toward: For one field crop and one vegetable, you will choose certified seed or clean planting material, the spacing and the planting or transplanting date, with each choice taken from a dealer, extension or the seed packet.
Good seed is the cheapest way to raise yield. Buy certified seed of a variety suited to your area from a registered dealer, and check the packet date and seal. For cassava, use clean cuttings from healthy plants, because virus diseases spread through infected cuttings.
Spacing decides how many plants share the light, water and nutrients. Use the spacing recommended for your variety and area, for example rows and plant distances for maize, and wider spacing in drier areas. Gaps and crowding both lose yield. Plant promptly once the rains have truly started and the soil is moist deep down.
Vegetables such as tomatoes, kale and onions are usually raised in a nursery first: a raised, well-drained bed or seedling trays, with clean soil, shade at first, careful watering and protection from pests. Harden seedlings by slowly giving more sun and less water before transplanting them, ideally in the cool evening.
Step by step:
- Buy certified seed (or clean cuttings) of a suitable variety.
- Use the recommended spacing for your variety and area.
- Plant when rains have truly started and soil is moist.
- Raise vegetable seedlings in a clean, well-drained nursery.
- Harden seedlings, then transplant in the cool evening.
Words to know:
- Certified seed: seed checked by the official seed authority for quality and variety.
- Spacing: the distance between rows and between plants.
- Nursery: a small, protected area where seedlings are raised before transplanting.
- Hardening: slowly getting seedlings used to field conditions before transplanting.
Official sources:
- Kenya Agricultural and Livestock Research Organization (KALRO)
Try it now: For your main field crop and one vegetable, write: the variety, where you will buy certified seed, the recommended spacing (ask an agrovet or extension officer), and your planned planting or transplanting date.
You can now plant a field crop and raise vegetable seedlings with good seed, spacing and timing.

check.q: Why should cassava be planted from clean cuttings of healthy plants?
options: Virus diseases spread through infected cuttings
Clean cuttings grow without water
Healthy plants need no spacing
Cuttings from sick plants cost more
check.why: Cassava virus diseases spread through infected cuttings, so clean cuttings from healthy plants protect the new crop.

check.q: Your tomato seedlings are ready in the nursery. What do you do before transplanting?
options: Water them twice as much
Move them straight into full sun at noon
Harden them with more sun and less water, then transplant in the cool evening
Cut off all their leaves
check.why: Hardening prepares seedlings for the field, and the cool evening reduces transplant shock.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Feeding the crop: manure, compost and fertilizer
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Plan how to feed a crop with organic and mineral nutrients, placed and timed well.
This lesson builds toward: For your main field crop, you will write a feeding plan that combines organic matter, legumes and well-placed fertilizer, with rates marked as coming from a soil test or extension.
Crops need nitrogen (N), phosphorus (P) and potassium (K), plus smaller amounts of other nutrients. Manure and compost add some nutrients and, just as importantly, organic matter that holds water and feeds soil life. Legumes such as beans, cowpea and groundnut add nitrogen to the soil through their roots.
Mineral fertilizers give nutrients quickly and in known amounts. A common pattern for maize is a planting fertilizer with phosphorus, then a nitrogen topdressing when the crop is knee-high, but the right products and rates depend on your soil test and local recommendations. Placing small amounts close to the plant (in the planting hole) uses fertilizer better than scattering it widely.
Combine both: organic matter plus well-placed fertilizer usually gives better and steadier yields than either alone. Make compost from crop residues, manure and kitchen waste, turned and kept moist. Never put fresh, hot manure or fertilizer directly on seed.
Step by step:
- Add manure or compost before or at planting.
- Include legumes in rotation or intercrop.
- Use fertilizer products and rates from your soil test and local recommendations.
- Place fertilizer near the plant, not touching seed.
- Topdress nitrogen at the right stage, when the soil is moist.
Words to know:
- N, P, K: nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium: the main plant nutrients.
- Topdressing: adding fertilizer, usually nitrogen, to a growing crop.
- Compost: decomposed plant and animal waste used to feed soil.
Official sources:
- FAO: Climate-Smart Agriculture Sourcebook (soil and water management)
- Kenya Agricultural and Livestock Research Organization (KALRO)
Try it now: Write a feeding plan for your field crop: what organic matter you will add and when, any legume, and the fertilizer products and timing (marked "rate from soil test or extension" if you do not know it yet). Start a compost heap if you do not have one.
You can now plan how to feed a crop with manure, compost and well-placed fertilizer.

check.q: What do manure and compost add besides nutrients?
options: Pesticide
Organic matter that holds water and feeds soil life
Certified seed
Lime
check.why: Organic matter holds water and feeds soil life, which is as important as the nutrients.

check.q: You have fertilizer for planting maize. Where do you put it?
options: In a small amount near the plant, not touching the seed
Scattered widely across the whole field
Directly on the seed
In a heap at the field edge
check.why: Placing small amounts near the plant uses fertilizer better, and fertilizer on seed can damage it.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Scouting and integrated pest management
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Scout a crop weekly and choose IPM actions before reaching for chemicals.
This lesson builds toward: Given a crop with pests or disease, you will scout it on a weekly routine, choose IPM actions and use a registered pesticide only by its label when justified, starting with prevention and non-chemical controls.
FAO describes integrated pest management (IPM) as considering all available pest control methods and combining the right ones, keeping pesticide use to what is justified. It starts with prevention: healthy soil, resistant varieties, clean seed, rotation, timely planting, field hygiene (removing infected plants and residues) and encouraging natural enemies such as ladybirds and parasitic wasps.
Scout every week. Walk a W or zigzag pattern through the field, check a set number of plants (for example 10 plants at 5 spots), and record what you see: fall armyworm damage in maize funnels, aphids, whiteflies, leaf spots, wilting, tomato leaf miner. Compare with what extension advises as the level where action is worth it.
Use non-chemical controls first where they work: hand-picking, push-pull for maize and sorghum, traps, neem-based or biological products approved for use, and removing infected plants. Fall armyworm sightings can be recorded with FAO's FAMEWS app where it is used. Get a diagnosis from an extension officer or plant clinic when you are unsure.
Step by step:
- Prevent: resistant varieties, clean seed, rotation, field hygiene.
- Scout weekly in a W pattern; check a set number of plants.
- Record pests, diseases and damage.
- Compare with extension's action levels.
- Use non-chemical controls first; get a diagnosis when unsure.
Words to know:
- IPM: integrated pest management: combining prevention, monitoring and many control methods, with pesticides only when justified.
- Scouting: walking the field regularly to check for pests and diseases.
- Natural enemies: insects and other creatures that eat or attack pests.
- Action level: the amount of pest or damage at which control is worth the cost.
Official sources:
- FAO: Integrated Pest Management
- icipe: Push-pull technology halts fall armyworm
- FAO: mobile application to support the fight against Fall Armyworm in Africa (FAMEWS)
Try it now: Make a weekly scouting sheet (date, spot, plants checked, pests, diseases, damage, action) and scout one field or vegetable bed this week.
You can now scout a crop weekly and choose IPM actions starting with prevention and non-chemical controls.

check.q: Which is a prevention step in IPM?
options: Spraying every week just in case
Buying a stronger pesticide
Mixing two pesticides together
Using resistant varieties and removing infected plants
check.why: IPM starts with prevention: resistant varieties, clean seed, rotation and field hygiene.

check.q: You find a few fall armyworm in your maize. What do you do first?
options: Spray the whole farm today
Record it and compare with the action level from extension
Ignore it until harvest
Burn the field
check.why: Scouting records are compared with the action level to decide whether control is worth it.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Safe, legal pesticide use and watering vegetables
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Use a pesticide safely when it is justified, and plan efficient watering for a vegetable plot.
This lesson builds toward: Given a crop with pests or disease, you will scout it on a weekly routine, choose IPM actions and use a registered pesticide only by its label when justified, starting with prevention and non-chemical controls. For a small vegetable plot, you will plan efficient watering with drip or cans, mulch and the right time of day, checking soil moisture before each watering.
If a pesticide is needed, use only products registered for that crop and pest in your country (in Kenya by the Pest Control Products Board; in Nigeria by NAFDAC), bought from a licensed dealer, never repacked in unlabelled bottles. Read the label and follow it exactly: rate, mixing, protective clothing, re-entry time and the pre-harvest interval, the number of days between spraying and harvest. Keep children and animals away, never eat or smoke while spraying, and dispose of containers safely, not as water or food containers.
Vegetables are thirsty and sensitive. Drip irrigation puts water at the roots, saves water and keeps leaves dry, which reduces disease in tomatoes. Low-cost drip kits and watering cans work for small plots. Water in the early morning or evening, and water deeply and less often rather than a little every day.
Mulch around vegetables to keep moisture in and soil off the leaves. Check soil moisture with your finger a few centimetres down before watering. Where water is scarce, collect rainwater from roofs and use water pans.
Step by step:
- Use only registered products for that crop and pest, from licensed dealers.
- Read and follow the label: rate, protective clothing, re-entry, pre-harvest interval.
- Dispose of containers safely.
- Water vegetables at the roots (drip or can), morning or evening.
- Mulch and check soil moisture before watering.
Words to know:
- Pre-harvest interval (PHI): the number of days you must wait after spraying before harvesting.
- Registered pesticide: a product approved by the national regulator for a stated use.
- Drip irrigation: watering through pipes with small holes that drip water at the roots.
Official sources:
- Pest Control Products Board (Kenya)
- National Agency for Food and Drug Administration and Control (NAFDAC, Nigeria)
- FAO: Integrated Pest Management
Try it now: Take any pesticide label (from a shop, the internet or your store). Write down: the crops and pests it is registered for, the rate, the protective clothing, and the pre-harvest interval. Then write a watering plan for your vegetable plot.
You can now use a pesticide safely and legally when justified, and water vegetables efficiently.

check.q: What is the pre-harvest interval on a pesticide label?
options: The time to mix the spray
The days before planting
The days to wait between spraying and harvest
The shelf life of the bottle
check.why: The pre-harvest interval is the number of days between the last spray and harvest.

check.q: Your kale plot is dry and you have a watering can. When do you water?
options: At midday, a little every hour
Early morning or evening, after checking soil moisture
Only after the leaves have wilted for a week
Never; wait for rain
check.why: Watering in the early morning or evening, deeply and only when the soil is dry, saves water and suits vegetables.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Harvest and post-harvest handling
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Harvest at the right time and handle, sort and store produce so it keeps its value.
This lesson builds toward: At harvest, you will plan how to harvest, sort, dry and store produce to cut losses, with the right maturity, gentle handling and safe storage for each crop.
Much food is lost after harvest. Harvest at the right maturity: tomatoes at the stage your buyer wants (often turning colour for distant markets), kale leaves young and tender, maize when the grain is mature and dry enough, cassava when roots are ready and only as much as you can sell or process quickly, because roots spoil within days.
Handle gently: use clean crates, not sacks, for tomatoes and soft produce; keep produce in the shade; and harvest in the cool morning. Sort and grade by size and quality, and remove damaged items so they do not spoil the rest. Respect the pre-harvest interval after any spraying.
Dry grain well before storage: damp maize and groundnuts can grow moulds that produce aflatoxin, a poison. Ask your buyer or extension officer for the target moisture and test it if you can. Store grain in clean, dry, raised stores or hermetic (airtight) storage bags to control weevils without chemicals.
Step by step:
- Harvest at the right maturity for your buyer.
- Harvest in the cool morning; keep produce in shade.
- Use clean crates for soft produce.
- Sort and grade; remove damaged items.
- Dry grain well; store in clean, dry, raised stores or hermetic bags.
Words to know:
- Post-harvest loss: food lost or spoiled between harvest and sale or use.
- Grading: sorting produce by size and quality.
- Aflatoxin: a poison made by moulds on damp grain and nuts.
- Hermetic bag: an airtight storage bag that stops insects by cutting off air.
Official sources:
- FAO: Integrated Pest Management
Try it now: Final task: write your season production plan for a field crop and a vegetable plot: soil checks and test, soil preparation and feeding, seed and spacing, planting dates, weekly scouting and IPM steps, vegetable watering, and harvest, sorting, storage and sale.
You can now harvest, handle, sort and store produce to cut losses and keep its value.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Soil checks No soil check or soil test is mentioned. Field check results are written down, with where and how a soil test sample would be taken. Uses soil test results, or a date to get one, to shape the plan. Seed, spacing and dates Seed source, spacing or planting dates are missing. Certified seed or clean material, recommended spacing and planting dates for both crops, with the source of each. Includes the nursery and hardening plan for the vegetable. Feeding the soil Only fertilizer is listed, or rates are guessed. Organic matter, any legume and fertilizer timing and placement, with rates from a soil test or extension. Includes a compost plan and a rotation for next season. Scouting and IPM Plans to spray on a schedule with no scouting. A weekly scouting routine, the main pests to watch, prevention and non-chemical steps, and label rules for any pesticide. Names where to get a diagnosis and the action level for one main pest. Watering No watering plan for the vegetables. Watering method, time of day, mulch and a soil-moisture check. Includes a way to collect or save water. Harvest and storage Harvest, sorting or storage is missing. Harvest timing, gentle handling, sorting, drying and storage and where to sell. Names the buyer's quality needs and how losses will be tracked. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part of the plan and check it again.

options: A fertilizer
A storage bag
A type of weevil
A poison from moulds on damp grain
check.why: Damp maize and groundnuts can grow moulds that produce aflatoxin, a poison.

check.q: You are harvesting tomatoes to sell. How do you carry them?
options: In clean crates, kept in the shade
In sacks in the sun
Piled loose in the cart
In a bag with the damaged ones
check.why: Clean crates and shade protect soft produce; sacks and sun bruise and spoil it.
